about_title: Malabar Hill, Mumbai - Mumbai's Most Elevated & Prestigious Residential Neighbourhood
about: Malabar Hill is where Mumbai looks down on itself - literally and figuratively. Perched on a promontory overlooking the Arabian Sea and Marine Drive, it is the city's most elevated and prestigious residential neighbourhood. Home to the Hanging Gardens, the ancient Banganga Tank, the Walkeshwar Temple, the Maharashtra Chief Minister's official residence and some of the most expensive real estate in India, it is a neighbourhood of extraordinary natural beauty, deep spiritual heritage and absolute social prestige. Whether you need a dentist near Ridge Road, a salon on B.G. character_vibe_description: Character & Vibe An honest snapshot - the energy, the people, the pace. The kind of thing no other directory tells you. Malabar Hill is Mumbai at its most elevated - in every sense. The streets are quiet. The air is cleaner. The views are extraordinary. And the residents move through their days with the unhurried confidence of people who have always lived at the top of the city. This is not a neighbourhood that announces itself. It simply is. The morning walkers at the Hanging Gardens, the devotees at the Banganga Tank, the children at the Kamala Nehru Park, the politicians at Varsha - they all share the same hill, the same sea breeze and the same extraordinary views. Malabar Hill is the only place in Mumbai where you can watch the Queen's Necklace from above, where the ancient and the ultra-modern coexist without friction, and where the city's most powerful people live alongside its most sacred sites.

resident_profile_description: Resident Profile Mumbai's most distinguished residents - here's who you'll find calling Malabar Hill home. Malabar Hill is home to some of Mumbai's - and India's - most powerful and distinguished families. The Maharashtra Chief Minister lives at Varsha on B.G. Kher Marg. Senior politicians, judges of the Bombay High Court, industrialists and old Parsi families have called this hill home for generations. The Hanging Gardens are their morning walk. The Banganga Tank is their spiritual anchor. And the view of Marine Drive from their windows is their daily reminder of why there is nowhere else in Mumbai quite like this.

faq.question: What is Malabar Hill known for?
faq.answer: Malabar Hill is known for being Mumbai's most prestigious and elevated residential neighbourhood, home to the Hanging Gardens, the ancient Banganga Tank, the Walkeshwar Temple, the Maharashtra Chief Minister's official residence (Varsha), and some of the most expensive real estate in India. It offers panoramic views of Marine Drive and the Arabian Sea.

faq.question: What are the sub-areas within Malabar Hill?
faq.answer: The main micro-localities within Malabar Hill are Hanging Gardens, Banganga Tank, Ridge Road, Teen Batti, Walkeshwar, Laburnum Road, B.G. Kher Marg, and the Malabar Hill Club belt.

faq.question: What is the property price in Malabar Hill?
faq.answer: Property prices in Malabar Hill are among the highest in India - ranging from ₹8 Cr for a 2BHK in the lower Malabar Hill belt to ₹20–50 Cr for a premium apartment on Ridge Road or B.G. Kher Marg, and ₹50 Cr+ for bungalows and penthouses. Rental rates range from ₹1.5 lakh to ₹5 lakh+ per month (as of May 2026).

faq.question: How to commute from Malabar Hill?
faq.answer: Malabar Hill is primarily served by private cars and taxis. The nearest Western Railway stations are Charni Road (15 min walk) and Grant Road (15 min walk). BEST bus routes 1, 83, 106, 132 serve the area. The Bandra-Worli Sea Link is accessible via Worli in 15 minutes.

faq.question: Which hospitals are in Malabar Hill?
faq.answer: Major hospitals in and near Malabar Hill include Breach Candy Hospital, Jaslok Hospital, Wockhardt Hospital, Saifee Hospital, and Bombay Hospital.

faq.question: Which schools are in Malabar Hill?
faq.answer: Notable schools near Malabar Hill include Campion School, Greenlawns High School, Walsingham House School, Cathedral & John Connon School, and Children's Academy.
